pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

5	
6	# Plan Regression Guard
7	
8	## Open with one line
9	"I'll list what the current version has and what it must say, make the change, then show you a kept / changed / removed check and a content-coverage result so nothing is lost."
10	
11	## When it runs (full trigger list)
12	The description carries the main phrases; this is the full list, kept for the
13	trigger tests. Edit, revise, update or make a new version of something that
14	already exists: "update the plan", "v3 of this", "add X to the training plan",
15	"revise this", "make these changes", "new version", "apply fixes 2 and 4",
16	"update the file", "update the page / app / doc", "fix it in the file",
17	"apply the fixes", "更新", "修改一下", "改这个文件", "出新版本", "按这个改".
18	A discussion or research report turned into a plan, doc, page or app: "build it
19	from what we discussed", "put the research into the page". A hand-over from
20	hz-reviewer when he now wants the change made.
21	
22	## The problem this solves
23	
24	When an artifact is edited version-to-version, features get lost silently. This happens because an edit regenerates the artifact from whatever is in working attention — not from a diff against the prior version. A feature that isn't actively re-stated can fall out, and nobody notices until much later. The user explicitly has no reliable way to catch this. This skill IS that reliable way.
25	
26	There is a second leak. Content agreed across a long conversation (a rule, a number, a caveat, a section) lives in many earlier messages, documents and reports. When a new version is built from the latest summary, points with no home in that summary fall out — and tests that check the artifact *works* cannot see that it is *incomplete*. So the guard keeps two lists, not one:
27	
28	- **Feature manifest** — what the artifact *does* (tabs, rules, formulas, behaviors).
29	- **Content ledger** — what the artifact must *say*: every point agreed in the conversation, each with a search phrase that must appear in the artifact. See `references/content-ledger.md`.
30	
31	There is a third leak, after a review: a problem shown in a review table can be
32	left out of the fixes, fixed only in part, or "fixed" without getting better,
33	and he cannot tell. When the change applies review fixes, the guard also proves
34	each finding's result (see "Findings closed" below).
35	
36	## The core discipline
37	
38	Every edit follows the same three-phase loop. Do not skip a phase, even for small edits — small edits are where features quietly drop.
39	
40	### Phase 1 — Extract the manifest (BEFORE editing anything)
41	
42	A **manifest** is the list of locked, non-negotiable features the current version has. Before making any change:
43	
44	1. Locate the manifest if one exists (see "Where the manifest lives" below).
45	   **For a skill package** (an hz- skill): first compare with the installed copy
46	   (`/mnt/skills/plugins/<skill>`) and search past chats for a newer package of
47	   the same skill (`conversation_search "<skill> package"`). If another chat built
48	   a newer one, name it and merge its changes first; never build on an older base.
49	   Deliver only the new package as a card. Never share a rollback as a card: keep
50	   the rollback file in the chat and send it only when he writes "roll back <skill>".
51	2. If no manifest exists yet, BUILD one by reading the current version end-to-end and listing every distinct feature, behavior, rule, section, or capability. State this list to the user and ask them to confirm/correct it before proceeding. This one-time cost prevents every future regression.
52	3. **Add his Mandatory requests.** Run steps 1–3 of the repeat check
53	   (`/mnt/skills/plugins/hz-reviewer/references/check-repeat.md`; if missing:
54	   read all his messages in this chat, group the same request in any words,
55	   count, and mark 3+ mentions Mandatory). Add each Mandatory request to the
56	   manifest as `Mandatory (said N×)`. A Mandatory item can only leave the
57	   manifest if he reverses it in a later message.
58	4. Hold the manifest as the checklist for this edit.
59	   **Impact list.** Before editing, name every file and section this change will
60	   touch, and show it in one line. A file or section touched outside that list
61	   is a regression, the same as a lost feature. Never delete, empty or rename a
62	   file that is not on the list.
63	   For each item you remove, rename or make stricter (a rule, a check, a
64	   feature, a version name), also list what reads or relies on it: checks,
65	   tests, documents, messages, version mentions. Prove each still works, or
66	   change it in the same version.
67	   **Review findings.** When the change applies review fixes, copy every finding
68	   ID from the review (R1, F2, L3…) onto the impact list, each with its type
69	   (fix or mitigation) and its expected result. Measure the "before" number now
70	   for every ID that has one.
71	5. Build or update the **content ledger**. Sweep the WHOLE conversation and every earlier source (earlier versions, docs, research reports, notes, and earlier chats this work came from: a handoff, or chats he names — search and read them) — never only the latest summary — and give each agreed point one line with a search phrase that must appear in the artifact. From then on, add a ledger line in the same turn a new point is agreed.
72	
73	A feature is anything a future reader would miss if it vanished: a scoring rule, a UI tab, a section, a formula, a constraint, a phase of the plan, a special case ("export only for admins"), a data field, an export option.
74	
75	### Phase 2 — Make the requested change
76	
77	Apply exactly what the user asked for. If the change intentionally *removes* a manifest feature, that's fine — but call it out explicitly in Phase 3 as an intentional removal, not a silent one. Update the manifest to reflect intentional additions and removals.
78	
79	Whenever a ledger item will not be in the new version (cut while condensing or simplifying, or found missing and not restored), list it under **Left out — OK?** and ask each one as a line in the answer's decision list. Never drop an agreed point silently; a cut is the user's decision, not a side effect of shortening.
80	
81	### Phase 3 — Verify against the manifest (BEFORE delivering)
82	
83	Compare what changed with the impact list: any file or section changed outside it is `❌ MISSING`-level and must be undone or confirmed. Walk the manifest item by item against the new version. For each item, confirm it is present and intact. Then report using the regression table format below. NEVER deliver a new version without this check.
84	
85	**Check every changed file.** Run the artifact's own check (layout check for a page, tests for code) on every file the change touched, not only the main one. A file changed but not checked is unproven.
86	
87	**Measure the result.** For every review ID, measure the "after" number the
88	same way as the "before" number, and compare it with the expected result.
89	
90	Then run the coverage gate on the content ledger: `python3 /mnt/skills/plugins/hz-change-guard/scripts/coverage_gate.py <artifact-file> [ledger-file]` (in chat; elsewhere use this skill's own `scripts/` folder). It prints every ledger phrase missing from the artifact and exits with an error if any is missing. Any MISSING line means STOP — fix it or move it to "Left out — OK?" for the user to confirm.
91	
92	**Find all, fix together, check once.** Finish the whole manifest walk and the whole gate run before fixing anything. Collect every `❌` row and every MISSING line into one list. Fix them all in one pass, then run the walk and the gate once more. One pass counts as one try for "Stop after 3 tries". For an artifact that only exists in chat, run the same check by hand against the ledger. Tests showing the artifact works are not proof it is complete; only the gate is.
93	
94	## Revision gate (every package for an hz- skill or a repo)
95	Runs before any package, zip or pull request is handed over, in every chat,
96	whether or not a trigger phrase started this skill. Each artifact keeps a
97	revision record inside it (`references/revision-record.md` for a skill;
98	`FEATURES.md` plus its open-problems list for a repo): version, the version it
99	was built on, owner, features with search phrases, open problems, fixed problems.
100	
101	Run `python3 /mnt/skills/plugins/hz-change-guard/scripts/revision_gate.py <new> <base>`.
102	`<base>` is the newest real copy: the installed skill (`/mnt/skills/plugins/<skill>`)
103	or a fresh clone of GitHub main. Never a copy from this chat's memory or uploads.
104	1. **Base check.** "Built on" in the new record must equal the base's Version.
105	   A newer base means another build happened: stop, rebuild on the base.
106	2. **Feature check.** Every feature in the base record is in the new record (or
107	   under "Removed (approved, with reason)"), and every phrase is in the new files.
108	3. **Problem check.** Every open problem in the base record is still open in the
109	   new record or moved to Fixed with its proof. None is dropped.
110	Any FAIL means STOP: fix it, or ask him as a decision. Show the gate's last line.
111	
112	**One owner.** Only the chat named in "Owner" builds the next package of that
113	artifact. Another chat that finds a problem or a new point does not build: it
114	gives him one open-problem line to paste into the owner chat. He can move the
115	owner by saying so.
116	
117	## Output format
118	
119	End every edit with this block:
120	
121	```
122	## Regression check — v{old} → v{new}
123	| Feature | Status |
124	|---|---|
125	| {feature 1} | ✅ kept |
126	| {feature 2} | ✅ kept |
127	| {feature 3} | ➕ added this version |
128	| {feature 4} | ⚠️ intentionally removed (you asked to drop X) |
129	| {feature 5} | ❌ MISSING — was this meant to go? |
130	```
131	
132	Under the table, add two lines:
133	
134	```
135	Content ledger: {present}/{total} present (coverage gate)
136	Left out — OK?: {cut items for the user to confirm, or "none"}
137	```
138	
139	A Mandatory row reads `✅ kept (Mandatory, said N×)`; one that is weakened or gone is `❌`.
140	
141	A missing ledger item counts exactly like a `❌ MISSING` feature.
142	
143	Any `❌ MISSING` line means STOP — surface it to the user and fix or confirm before considering the edit done. A `⚠️` line is allowed only if the user explicitly asked to remove that feature this turn.
144	
145	### Findings closed (when the change applies review fixes)
146	Add one more table, one row per finding ID from the review, none skipped:
147	
148	```
149	| ID | Problem | Type · how | Expected | Actual | Status | Proof |
150	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
151	| F2 | open item answer goes nowhere | Fix · 4-step rule | 100% | 100% | ✅ Closed | phrase found |
152	| R2 | 27 cost blanks | Mitigation · web prices | 30% fewer | 30% fewer (27 → 19) | ⚠️ Mitigated: 19 wait for quotes | count |
153	| T1 | 18 min per check run | Fix · changed pages only | 65% faster (est.) | 40% faster (18 → 11 min) | ⚠️ Below expected: big page still slow | timer |
154	| R6 | upload the Project file | Your action | — | — | 👤 Your action | — |
155	| G1 | nothing saves | Not fixing · needs the repo | — | — | ⏭ Roadmap | — |
156	```
157	
158	- **Status** is one of ✅ Closed · ⚠️ Mitigated (say what remains) ·
159	  ⚠️ Below expected (say why, and the next step) · 👤 Your action ·
160	  ⏭ Not fixing (reason and when it comes back).
161	- **Actual** is measured, not copied from Expected. When it can't be measured
162	  yet, write "not measured" and say when and how it will be.
163	- Under the table add one count line: "Findings N · closed N · mitigated N ·
164	  below expected N · your action N · not fixing N".
165	- The edit is not done while any review ID is missing from this table.
166	
167	## Where the manifest lives (by format)
168	
169	The discipline is identical across formats; only the storage location changes.
170	
171	- **Text/markdown/Word doc** → an HTML comment block or a "Locked Features" section pinned at the top. See `references/manifest-formats.md`.
172	- **App / code** → a header comment block at the top of the main file, e.g. `<!-- FEATURE MANIFEST v3: offline cache; weekly reset; parent PIN; ... -->`.
173	- **Spreadsheet** → a frozen top block or a dedicated `_Manifest` sheet.
174	- **Pasted-in-chat plan with no file** → there's nowhere to pin it, so hold the manifest in the conversation, restate it at the top of each new version, and run the regression check in chat every turn.
175	
176	The content ledger sits right next to the manifest, in the same place and the same format family (see `references/content-ledger.md`).
177	
178	Read `references/manifest-formats.md` for the exact template per format and for how to bootstrap a manifest on an artifact that doesn't have one yet.
179	
180	## Versioning
181	
182	Always label versions explicitly (v1, v2, v3b — match whatever scheme the user already uses). The regression table header references the old and new version numbers so the user can trace what changed when.
183	
184	**Plan discussion rounds keep one version.** While a plan is still being discussed, each new round keeps the same version number and adds one change-log line ("Round 2: …"). Never make v2, v3, v4 before execution. The version closes only when he approves or says there are no more changes; the next change after that gets the next number. During rounds the table header reads `v{n} round {k} → round {k+1}`.
185	
186	## What NOT to do
187	
188	- Do not regenerate the whole artifact from memory and hope features survive. Diff against the manifest.
189	- Do not assume a feature is unimportant because the current edit doesn't touch it. Untouched features are exactly the ones that vanish.
190	- Do not skip the check on "trivial" edits.
191	- Do not silently improve or "clean up" features the user didn't ask you to change.
192	- Do not build a new version from the latest source alone (a summary, a research report). Points agreed earlier in the conversation live elsewhere; the ledger sweep finds them.
193	- Do not treat "it renders" or "the tests pass" as proof the content is complete.
194	- Do not report review fixes by fix number alone; report each finding ID, its expected and actual result, and its status.
195	- Do not call a mitigation a fix: say what remains.
196	
197	## Checks reminder
198	After every new version of an app or design, end with one line listing the
199	checks not run this turn: "Checks not run: flow ☐ logic ☐ repeat ☐ — say
200	'run all checks' to run all three at once." (Repeat counts as run when the
201	manifest step above ran it.)
202	
203	## Stop after 3 tries
204	If the same check (gate, test, layout check) fails 3 times on the same item,
205	stop fixing. Report the item, the 3 attempts, and the likely cause, then wait.
206	A new approach needs his OK; repeating the same fix is not a 4th try.
207	
208	## Evidence before "done"
209	A version is "done" only when the proof is shown, not claimed: the regression
210	table with every item ticked, plus the artifact-specific proof — test output,
211	a row count, a screenshot, a rendered page — plus the coverage gate output
212	for the content ledger, plus the revision gate output for a package, plus the findings-closed table with measured results
213	when review fixes were applied. No proof, no "done"; say what is still
214	unproven and how to prove it.
215	
216	## Revision record
217	Approved features, open problems and fixes: `references/revision-record.md`.
218	Any change to this skill updates that record in the same build, and the
219	hz-change-guard revision gate runs before the package is handed over.
